m1-laws: State Ohm’s law, with its condition.
At constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it and inversely proportional to its resistance: I = V/R, V = IR, R = V/I.
At a node, the algebraic sum of currents is zero: total current entering = total current leaving. It is conservation of charge.
Around a closed loop, the algebraic sum of voltage drops and sources is zero: sum of rises = sum of drops. It is conservation of energy.
Node a has I<sub>1</sub> entering and I<sub>2</sub>, I<sub>3</sub>, I<sub>4</sub> leaving. Write KCL.
I<sub>1</sub> = I<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>3</sub> + I<sub>4</sub>, or I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>2</sub> − I<sub>3</sub> − I<sub>4</sub> = 0.
Loop abcda: battery V, R<sub>1</sub> carrying I<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> carrying I<sub>3</sub>. Write KVL.
Which three laws does the course list for electrical circuits?
Ohm’s law, Kirchhoff’s laws (KCL and KVL) and Faraday’s laws.
Why does Ohm’s law need constant temperature?
Resistance changes with temperature. Only with R fixed is V proportional to I.
You guessed a current direction and the answer came out negative. What does that mean?
The real current flows the other way, with the same size. The working is still correct.
m1-series-parallel: Give the five characteristics of a series connection.
Same current through all; each drop depends on its own R; R<sub>eff</sub> = sum of R; applied V = sum of drops; total power = sum of powers.
Give the four characteristics of a parallel connection.
Same voltage across each; 1/R<sub>eff</sub> = sum of 1/R; total current = sum of branch currents; total power = sum of powers.
Current I splits between R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> in parallel. Current through R<sub>3</sub>?
IR3 = I × R2/(R2 + R3), the other branch on top.
Convert E<sub>s</sub> in series with R<sub>s</sub> into a current source.
Current source Is = Es/Rs with the same Rs in parallel.
Derive R<sub>eff</sub> for three resistors in series.

V = V<sub>1</sub> + V<sub>2</sub> + V<sub>3</sub> = I(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub> + R<sub>3</sub>) since the current is the same, so V/I = R<sub>eff</sub> = R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub> + R<sub>3</sub>.
Derive R<sub>eff</sub> for three resistors in parallel.

I = I<sub>1</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>3</sub> → V/R<sub>eff</sub> = V/R<sub>1</sub> + V/R<sub>2</sub> + V/R<sub>3</sub> (same V) → 1/R<sub>eff</sub> = 1/R<sub>1</sub> + 1/R<sub>2</sub> + 1/R<sub>3</sub>.
How do you tie resistors in series and in parallel, using marked polarities?
Series: tie alternate polarities (− to +). Parallel: tie the same polarities (+ to +, − to −). Resistors have no real polarity; the marks only help.
What does the V–R staircase graph of a series circuit show?
Potential falls by V<sub>1</sub>, V<sub>2</sub>, V<sub>3</sub> across R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, R<sub>3</sub> and stays flat along the wires, from A down to D.
Why is parallel R<sub>eff</sub> smaller than the smallest branch?
Each branch adds another path for current, so more current flows for the same voltage.
Circuit: R<sub>3</sub>∥R<sub>4</sub>∥R<sub>5</sub> in series with R<sub>1</sub>, that in parallel with R<sub>2</sub>, all in series with R<sub>6</sub>. R<sub>eq</sub>?
R<sub>eq</sub> = R<sub>6</sub> + R<sub>2</sub> ∥ [R<sub>1</sub> + (R<sub>3</sub>∥R<sub>4</sub>∥R<sub>5</sub>)].
m1-mesh: List the five steps of mesh (loop current) analysis.
1 Mark and name the nodes. 2 Mark a loop current in each loop (clockwise). 3 Write KVL for each loop. 4 Solve the simultaneous equations. 5 The solution gives the loop currents.
A 3 Ω is shared by loops carrying I<sub>1</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> (both clockwise). Its drop in loop 1’s equation?
(I1 − I2) × 3. The loop’s own current minus the neighbour’s.
How does Cramer’s rule give I<sub>2</sub> from [R][I] = [V]?
I2 = ΔI2/Δ, where ΔI2 is Δ with column 2 replaced by the [V] column.
Define loop, node and reference node.
Loop: a closed path for current. Node: a point where elements connect. Reference node: a node at low (zero) potential, common to all nodes.
Course mesh example: give the matrix equation.
Course mesh example: Δ, ΔI<sub>1</sub>, ΔI<sub>2</sub>, ΔI<sub>3</sub>?
Course mesh example: the three loop currents?
Which two things does the course’s mesh method leave out?
Controlled (dependent) sources and supermeshes.
Quick check of a mesh coefficient matrix?
Diagonal = total resistance in that loop; off-diagonal = minus the resistance shared by the two loops; the matrix is symmetric.
m1-nodal: List the steps of nodal voltage analysis.
1 Mark the principal nodes. 2 Pick the reference (zero) node. 3 Mark current directions. 4 Identify the graph (current paths). 5 Name V<sub>a</sub>, V<sub>b</sub>. 6 Write KCL at each node and solve.
Current from a 10 V source through 5 Ω into node a. Write it with node voltages.
I1 = (10 − Va)/5: tail voltage minus head voltage, over R.
Course nodal example: V<sub>a</sub> and V<sub>b</sub>?
What is a reference node?
One of the principal nodes, taken at zero potential and common to the remaining principal nodes.
Course nodal example: the two equations in clean form?
11V<sub>a</sub> − 3V<sub>b</sub> = 60 and −12V<sub>a</sub> + 37V<sub>b</sub> = 60.
Course nodal example: I<sub>1</sub> to I<sub>5</sub>?
What is the "graph" in step 4?
The circuit reduced to its nodes and the paths (resistances) joining them, showing where current can flow to the reference node.
Three ways to find power in a resistor?
P = VI, P = I2R, P = V2/R.
Mesh or nodal for the course example circuit, and why?
Nodal: only two unknown node voltages, versus three loop currents.
m1-thevenin: State Thevenin’s theorem.

In a linear, bilateral network, the current through a load RL across terminals A and B is IL = Voc/(Rin + RL), where Voc is the open-circuit voltage at A–B and Rin the resistance seen back from A–B with sources replaced by their internal resistances.
When finding R<sub>th</sub>, what happens to voltage sources and current sources?
Voltage sources → short circuit (or their internal resistance). Current sources → open circuit (infinite resistance).
Course exercise (10 V, 2 Ω, 4 Ω, 2 Ω, 4 Ω + 4 V): V<sub>th</sub>, R<sub>th</sub>, and I for 1 Ω and 2 Ω?
List the eight steps of applying Thevenin’s theorem.

1 Name nodes. 2 Remove R<sub>L</sub>. 3 Find V<sub>TH</sub> across AB. 4 Short voltage sources (keep r), open current sources. 5 Find R<sub>TH</sub> looking back. 6 Draw V<sub>TH</sub> with R<sub>TH</sub>. 7 Reconnect R<sub>L</sub> in series. 8 I = V<sub>TH</sub>/(R<sub>TH</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>).
V<sub>1</sub> with internal r, series R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> across A–B. R<sub>TH</sub>?
R<sub>TH</sub> = (R<sub>1</sub> + r)R<sub>2</sub>/[(R<sub>1</sub> + r) + R<sub>2</sub>].
What is V<sub>oc</sub> (V<sub>th</sub>)?
The voltage across A and B with the load removed: the open-circuit voltage.
What do "linear" and "bilateral" mean here?
Linear: resistances don’t change with current or voltage. Bilateral: they behave the same in both directions.
Why does Thevenin save time for several load values?
Vth and Rth are found once; each new RL needs only I = Vth/(Rth + RL).
Extra: for what load is the power maximum?
RL = Rth; Pmax = Vth2/(4Rth).
m1-superposition: In a network of linear resistances with more than one generator, the current at any point is the sum of the currents due to each generator acting separately, the others replaced by their internal resistances.
Superposition exercise (2.05 V/0.005 Ω, 2.15 V/0.04 Ω, R = 1 Ω): current in R?
Can you find power by superposition?
No. Power goes as I2. Add the currents first, then find power.
What replaces the other sources while one acts alone?
Resistances equal to their internal resistances (an ideal voltage source becomes a short circuit).
Why does superposition need a linear network?
Only then is each current proportional to its cause, so the effects of separate sources simply add.
Two contributions flow in opposite directions in a branch. Net current?
The difference, in the direction of the larger one.
Course figure (6 V/0.5 Ω, 2.5 Ω; 12 V/1 Ω, 2 Ω; 6 Ω middle): current in 6 Ω (Extra working)?
m1-ac-basics: What is one cycle of an alternating quantity?
One complete set of positive and negative values. In angular measure it spreads over 360° or 2π rad.
How are frequency and time period related?
f = 1/T, in cycles per second (Hz). Frequency is the number of cycles per second. At 50 Hz, T = 20 ms.
What is phase difference?
The fixed angle φ between two alternating quantities of the same frequency. The one that reaches its peak (or zero) first leads; the other lags.
Define time period T.
Time taken to complete one set of positive and negative values of the alternating quantity.
Amplitude vs peak amplitude (as defined in the course)?
Amplitude: the instantaneous peak value, + or −. Peak amplitude Am: the maximum peak value, + or −.
How does a rotating phasor give a sine wave?
A line of length Im rotates at ω; its vertical projection at angle θ is i = Im sin θ.
What is the peak-to-peak value of a sine wave?
From +Amax to −Amax: 2Amax.
Write ω in terms of f. What is it for 50 Hz?
Equation of a wave that leads A<sub>m</sub> sin ωt by φ?
Am sin(ωt + φ). A lagging wave is Am sin(ωt − φ).
m1-ac-values: Define the RMS value of an alternating current.
The steady DC current which, through 1 Ω for t seconds, produces the same heat as the AC current does in the same time.
RMS and average values of a sine wave in terms of peak?
Vrms = Vm/√2 = 0.707 Vm; Vav = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm (half cycle).
Form factor and crest factor of a sine wave?
Form factor = rms/average = 1.11. Crest (peak, amplitude) factor = max/rms = 1.414.
Two methods of finding RMS and average values?
(i) Mid-ordinate method (ii) analytical method.
Mid-ordinate formula for RMS?
V<sub>rms</sub> = √[(V<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> + V<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> + … + V<sub>n</sub><sup>2</sup>)/n] using equally spaced mid-ordinates.
Why is the average of a sine wave taken over half a cycle?
Over a full cycle the positive and negative halves cancel, so the average is zero.
What slip is in the course RMS derivation?
It repeats the average working and ends at 0.637 Vm. Correct: Vrms2 = (1/2π)∫Vm2sin2θ dθ = Vm2/2, so 0.707 Vm.
50 Hz, 20 A rms: instantaneous equation?
v = 282.8 sin 314t: RMS, f and v at 4 ms?
Why square the values for RMS?
Heating goes as i2R, which does not care about direction; squaring makes both halves count.
m1-rl-series: R-L series: write X<sub>L</sub>, Z and power factor.
XL = ωL = 2πfL; Z = √(R2 + XL2); pf = cos φ = R/Z (lagging), 0 < pf < 1.
Active, reactive and apparent power?
P = VI cos φ (W); Q = VI sin φ (VAR); S = VI = √(P2 + Q2) (VA).
Q factor of a coil (course definition)? Standard one?
Course: Q = 1/pf = Z/R. Standard: Q = XL/R = ωL/R; nearly equal when XL ≫ R.
In an R-L circuit, how is the current placed relative to V?
It lags V by φ, where tan φ = XL/R.
Why is Z not simply R + X<sub>L</sub>?
VR and VX are 90° apart, so they add as the sides of a right triangle.
What do +P and −P areas on the R-L power curve mean?
+P: energy taken from the supply. −P: energy the coil returns to the supply. Net (average) power = VI cos φ.
Ex 3 choke (2 A lagging 60° at 200 V, 50 Hz): R, L, Z?
Z = 100 Ω, R = 50 Ω, L = 0.275 H; on 100 V, 25 Hz it takes 114.3 W (course prints 112.5 W).
How do you get a coil's R and X from a test at V, I, P?
Z = V/I, R = P/I2, X = √(Z2 − R2).
Ex 6: X<sub>L</sub> = 1.25 Ω at 25 Hz, supply ω = 377. What X<sub>L</sub> do you use?
What is wrong with Ex 7 as printed?
2202 is less than 1252 + 2002, so the coil would need negative resistance. The answers fit a 250 V supply (coil r 5.5 Ω, X 39.6 Ω).
m1-rc-rlc: R-L-C series: impedance formula?
Z = √(R2 + (XL ~ XC)2); the reactances subtract because they act in opposite directions.
Capacitive reactance formula, and what happens to it as f rises?
XC = 1/(2πfC); it falls as f rises (infinite at DC).
When does an R-L-C circuit have lagging, leading or unity pf?
XL > XC: lagging; XL < XC: leading; XL = XC: unity (resonance).
In an R-C circuit, how does current sit relative to V?
It leads V by φ, tan φ = XC/R; pf = R/Z leading.
Coil pf 0.6 + 100 µF, equal p.d. across both, 50 Hz: R and L?
XC = 31.83 Ω = Zcoil; R = 19.1 Ω, L = 81.1 mH (course prints 79.8 mH).
R 50 Ω, L 0.15 H, C 25 µF on 230 V 50 Hz: Z, I, pf?
Series capacitor that leaves a coil's current unchanged?
Needs XC = 2XL; for 8 Ω, 0.03 H at 50 Hz, C = 168.9 µF.
Resonant frequency of a series R-L-C circuit (Extra)?
fr = 1/(2π√LC); Z = R (minimum), current maximum, pf = 1.
Why can V<sub>C</sub> exceed the supply voltage in R-L-C?
VL and VC are 180° apart and largely cancel, so each can be large while their sum is small.
m1-fuse: What is a fuse and how is it connected?
A short length of wire designed to melt and separate on excessive current. Always connected in series with what it protects, so blowing opens the whole circuit.
Name the two high-voltage AC fuse types.
Expulsion fuse and HRC fuse.
How does a drop-out fuse work and what does it protect?
An expulsion type fuse protecting transformers; when the element melts the tube falls by gravity, giving extra isolation.
Five types of DC fuse?
Cartridge, automotive, resettable, semiconductor, over-voltage suppression.
Five types of low-voltage AC fuse?
Cartridge, drop-out, rewireable, striker, switch.
Liquid HV HRC fuse: what liquid, and what does it do?
Carbon tetrachloride in a glass tube with brass caps; it acts as the arc extinguishing medium. A phosphor bronze spring holds the wire.
What is in the chamber of an expulsion HV fuse?
Boric acid; gases from internal arcing are expelled and interrupt the current. Used for feeders and transformers.
Parts of an HRC cartridge fuse?
Fuse element, outer element (body), fuse link contacts, brass end plates, filling powder.
Fusing factor (Extra)?
Minimum fusing current / current rating; always greater than 1.
Why does a fuse heat up so fast on overcurrent?
Heat goes as I2R: doubling the current gives four times the heat.
m1-earthing: What does an earthing system do?
Connects specific parts of an installation to the Earth's conductive surface for safety and functional purposes; the Earth is the reference point.
Plate earthing: plate size and depth?
60 × 60 cm × 6.3 mm GI or 60 × 60 cm × 3.15 mm copper, at least 150 cm below ground, in 15 cm of charcoal.
Pipe earthing: pipe size, length and fill?
38 mm φ GI pipe, 2.5 m (min), 12 mm holes 7.5 cm apart, alternate salt and charcoal layers of 15 cm.
How does earthing protect a person touching a faulty appliance?
Fault current flows through the low-resistance earth path, blowing the fuse; the body stays near earth potential.
Why charcoal and salt around the earth electrode?
Charcoal holds moisture; salt makes the wet soil more conductive. Both lower earth resistance.
What is the funnel in an earth pit for?
To pour water down to the electrode in dry weather; wire mesh keeps dirt out.
Plate earthing pipes?
Ø19 mm GI pipe to the plate; Ø12.7 mm GI pipe for the earth lead.
Depth to the top of the pipe in pipe earthing?
1.25 m (min); connecting pipe 19.05 mm φ GI.
Concrete mix of the plate-earthing chamber?
Cement concrete 1:4:8, with a GI cover hinged to a GI frame.
m1-dc-machine: Name the two ports of an electrical machine and what flows at each.
Mechanical port (shaft: torque and speed, power P<sub>mi</sub>) and electrical port (terminals: voltage e<sub>t</sub>, power P<sub>ei</sub>).
Long shunt vs short shunt compound machine?
Short shunt: shunt field across the armature only. Long shunt: shunt field across the armature and series field together.
Number of parallel paths A for lap and wave windings?
Lap: A = P (number of poles). Wave: A = 2.
Where is energy stored inside a rotating machine?
In the magnetic field and in the rotating mass.
What does the pole shoe do?
Spreads the flux over the armature surface and holds the field coil in place on the pole core.
List the parts in the DC machine cross-section.
Yoke, pole core, pole shoe, field coil, armature, armature conductors, shaft, base.
What are Y<sub>B</sub>, Y<sub>F</sub>, Y<sub>R</sub>, Y<sub>C</sub>?
Back pitch, front pitch, resultant pitch and commutator pitch of an armature winding.
Separately excited vs self excited?
Separately excited: field fed from a separate DC supply. Self excited: the machine supplies its own field (series, shunt or compound).
Why is the armature core laminated?
It rotates in the magnetic field; laminations cut down eddy currents and the heat they make.
m1-dc-generator: Write the EMF equation of a DC machine and name the symbols.
E<sub>g</sub> = PφZN/(60A). P poles, φ flux per pole (Wb), Z total conductors, N speed (rpm), A parallel paths.
Short-shunt generator: what voltage does the shunt field see?
Terminal voltage plus the series field drop: V + I<sub>L</sub>R<sub>se</sub>.
Shunt generator: how are I<sub>a</sub>, I<sub>L</sub>, I<sub>sh</sub> related?
I<sub>a</sub> = I<sub>L</sub> + I<sub>sh</sub>, with I<sub>sh</sub> = V/R<sub>sh</sub>.
In the EMF derivation, how much flux does one conductor cut per revolution, and how long does it take?
dφ = φP webers in dt = 60/N seconds, so emf per conductor = φPN/60 V.
Example 4.1 answer (shunt, 400 A at 220 V, R<sub>sh</sub> 250 Ω, R<sub>a</sub> 0.15 Ω)?
Example 4.2 (short shunt, 25 A at 230 V): correct emf and why the course answer differs?
239.55 V with I<sub>a</sub> = 26.18 A. The printed 239.845 V is the long-shunt result.
Example 4.3: flux per pole?
I<sub>a</sub> = 127 A, E<sub>g</sub> = 414.7 V, lap so A = 8: φ = 0.162 Wb.
What do slip rings give, and what does a commutator change?
Slip rings pass on the coil's alternating emf. A commutator reverses the coil connection each half turn so the output is DC.
How do you handle "1 V per brush"?
Two brushes, so add 2 V to the emf (generator).
m1-dc-motor: What is back emf and its equation?
The emf induced in a running motor's armature, opposing the supply: E<sub>b</sub> = V − I<sub>a</sub>R<sub>a</sub> = φZNP/(60A).
Armature torque of a DC motor?
T<sub>a</sub> = (1/2π) φZI<sub>a</sub>(P/A) = 0.159 φZI<sub>a</sub>(P/A) N·m.
Example 1 (8.2 kW series motor): speed and torques?
T<sub>a</sub> = 286.2 N·m, E<sub>b</sub> = 193 V, N = 289.5 rpm = 4.83 rps, T<sub>sh</sub> = 270.5 N·m (not the printed 43.52).
Speed formula from back emf?
N = E<sub>b</sub> × 60 × A / (φZP) rpm.
Shunt motor: armature current?
I<sub>a</sub> = I<sub>L</sub> − I<sub>sh</sub>.
Example 2 (220 V shunt motor, 540 lap conductors): speed and torque?
I<sub>a</sub> = 31 A, E<sub>b</sub> = 217.21 V, N = 804.5 rpm, T<sub>a</sub> = 79.9 N·m.
Starting point of the torque derivation?
Electrical power into the armature = mechanical power developed: E<sub>b</sub>I<sub>a</sub> = 2πN T<sub>a</sub> (N in rps).
Power in terms of torque, N in rps and in rpm?
P = T × 2πN (rps) = 2πNT/60 (rpm); P = Tω.
Why must a motor's coil current be opposite to a generator's for the same rotation?
The generator current makes a force that opposes the motion (Lenz). For the force to drive the motion, the current must be reversed.
Why is T<sub>sh</sub> less than T<sub>a</sub>?
Part of the developed torque is used up by the motor's own losses (friction, iron loss); T<sub>sh</sub> is what reaches the load.
m1-bldc: What rotates and what stays still in a BLDC motor?
The permanent-magnet rotor rotates; the armature coils (electromagnets) on the stator stay still.
What replaces the commutator in a BLDC motor?
Electronic switching: transistors switched by timing and drive circuitry that reads a rotor position (Hall effect) sensor.
Blocks of the BLDC drive circuit?

AC source → bridge rectifier D<sub>1</sub>–D<sub>4</sub> → capacitor C (DC) → transistors TR<sub>1</sub>–TR<sub>3</sub> → windings A, B, C (star point to +); rotor position sensor → timing and drive circuitry.
Two operating regions on the BLDC torque–speed curve?
Continuous (can run indefinitely) and intermittent (higher torque for short times).
What is the Hall effect sensor for?
It senses the rotor magnet position so the right winding is switched on at the right time.
Any four of: transport, cordless tools, heating and ventilation, motion control, positioning and actuation, aeromodelling, power converter, radio-controlled cars.
Chopping control is used at low speed (hatched region); angle control extends operation at high speed.
m1-transformer: A static device that transfers energy from one electrical network to another without changing the operating frequency, working on mutual induction.
E<sub>rms</sub> = 4.44 f N Φ<sub>max</sub>, from E = N dΦ/dt with Φ = Φ<sub>m</sub> sin ωt.
Core: L-shaped laminations, windings on the two side limbs. Shell: E + I laminations, both windings on the central limb, flux splits through the outer limbs.
Whichever winding the source is connected to; the other is the secondary.
What stays the same on the HV and LV sides?
The VA rating, at all instants; so voltage and current change in opposite directions.
Why won't a transformer work on DC?
Steady DC gives a constant flux; with no change in flux, no emf is induced in the secondary.
Times on the flux wave for Φ<sub>m</sub>, zero and one cycle?
Peak at 1/(4f), zero at 1/(2f), full cycle T = 1/f.
m1-induction-motor: How is a rotating magnetic field produced?
Three stator windings 120° apart in space carry three-phase currents 120° apart in time; the resultant flux has constant size and rotates.
Why does the rotor of an induction motor turn?
The rotating flux cuts the rotor bars and induces currents; the field acts on those currents, giving torque in the direction of the field.
Two types of three-phase induction motor rotor?
Squirrel cage rotor and wound rotor (slip ring).
Single-phase induction motor types listed in the course?
Split phase, capacitor start, shaded pole, hysteresis, reluctance and universal motors.
Always φ<sub>r</sub> = φ<sub>m</sub>, pointing a different way each time: constant magnitude, rotating.
Supply used in the principle diagram?
Finned frame, laminated slotted stator core, three-phase copper winding in the slots.
The rotor always runs slower than the rotating field; at the same speed no flux would be cut and no torque produced.
m1-drives: Blocks of a power-electronics-based electric drive?
Input supply, power module, motor, load, sensors, controller (with reference); PWM pulses from controller to power module.
Voltage and current to the motor, and its torque and speed.
The feedback signal from the sensors with the reference.
What signal goes from the controller to the power module?
Why is the drive called closed loop?
The output (torque, speed) is measured and fed back to the controller, which corrects the power module.
Switches are fully on or off, so little power is lost in them, and the on-time sets the average voltage.
m2-semiconductors: Why is pure (intrinsic) silicon a good insulator?
All its valence electrons are locked in covalent bonds in the crystal lattice, so there are no free carriers.
What is doping, and what is the doped material called?
Adding impurity atoms to a pure semiconductor so it conducts. The result is an extrinsic semiconductor.
Majority and minority carriers in N-type and in P-type?
N-type: electrons are majority, holes minority. P-type: holes are majority, electrons minority.
How does arsenic make silicon N-type?
Arsenic has 5 valence electrons. Four bond with silicon, and the fifth is free to conduct.
How does boron make silicon P-type?
Boron has 3 valence electrons, so one bond is incomplete. The missing electron place is a hole, which carries positive charge.
What happens to resistance as you add more dopant?
More free carriers, so lower resistance. Fewer dopant atoms give higher resistance.
The empty place where a bonding electron should be. It behaves as a positive charge carrier.
m2-pn-junction: What is the potential barrier of a silicon diode and of a germanium diode?
How does the potential barrier form?
Electrons diffuse to the P-side and holes to the N-side. The net opposite charge left in each layer stops further diffusion, setting up the barrier.
Battery positive to P-type, negative to N-type. Above V0 the barrier vanishes and large current flows.
What happens to the depletion region in reverse bias?
It becomes wider, and the barrier increases, so practically no current flows.
What is reverse saturation current and what does it depend on?
A very small (microamp) reverse current. It depends mainly on junction temperature, since thermally broken bonds are the source of minority carriers.
At large reverse bias, fast electrons knock out more valence electrons, producing an avalanche of free electrons and a very large reverse current.
What is the forward current when V_F < V_0?
Almost zero, because the barrier has not yet disappeared.
m2-diode-vi: Where is the knee voltage on a silicon and a germanium diode curve?
How big is the reverse leakage current in silicon and germanium diodes?
Less than 20 µA in silicon and less than 50 µA in germanium.
A device that converts AC to DC (one direction only). The process is rectification.
Why is a half-wave rectifier inefficient?
It blocks one half of the input, so only half the input waveform reaches the output.
What does a full-wave rectifier do differently?
It converts both polarities of the input to one polarity, so the whole waveform is used and it is more efficient.
Which diode terminal is the anode?
The arrow side (P side). The bar side is the cathode (N side).
m2-zener: A heavily doped silicon PN junction diode operated in the reverse breakdown region.
Why does an ordinary diode get damaged in breakdown but a Zener does not?
The Zener is designed with adequate power dissipation to operate safely in breakdown.
How does doping set the Zener breakdown voltage?
Heavier doping gives a thinner depletion layer, so breakdown is at a lower reverse voltage and is sharper.
Why can a Zener act as a voltage regulator?
In breakdown the voltage across it stays almost constant while the current changes, giving a reference voltage.
Condition for the Zener regulator to hold the load voltage?
The input voltage must not fall below V_Z; the Zener is reverse biased.
Range of Zener voltages and power ratings?
1.8 V to 200 V and ¼ W to 50 W.
Overvoltage protection and setting reference voltages.
m2-bjt-basics: Why is the BJT called bipolar?
Its operation depends on both majority and minority carriers (electrons and holes).
Which BJT region is heavily doped, and why?
The emitter, because it must supply majority carriers to the base.
Describe the base of a BJT.
The middle section, very thin and very lightly doped.
Why is the collector bigger than the emitter?
It has to dissipate much greater power. So the transistor cannot be used inverted.
Where is the arrowhead on a BJT symbol and what does it show?
Always on the emitter, showing the conventional current direction.
Bias conditions for the active region?
Emitter–base junction forward biased, collector–base junction reverse biased.
How is the emitter current split?
I_E = I_B + I_C. About 1–2 % goes to the base and 98–99 % to the collector.
NPN versus PNP in one line each?
NPN: two N regions around one P, arrow base to emitter. PNP: two P regions around one N, arrow emitter to base.
m2-bjt-operation: Why is the base current so small in an NPN transistor?
The base is thin and lightly doped P-type with few holes, so very few injected electrons recombine there.
What sweeps electrons from base to collector in an NPN?
The strong electric field of the reverse-biased collector junction. Almost 95 % get through.
Which carriers carry the main current in a PNP?
Holes, injected from the emitter. More than 95 % cross into the collector.
How does I_E relate to the other currents?
Which junction is forward biased and which reverse in normal operation?
Emitter–base is forward biased; collector–base is reverse biased.
What forms the base current in a PNP?
The few holes that combine with electrons in the N-type base.
m2-bjt-config: What does “common” mean in a configuration?
The electrode shared by the input and output circuits, usually grounded.
Which configuration gives the highest voltage, current and power gain?
What does the CE input characteristic plot?
I_B against V_BE with V_CE held constant.
What does the CE output characteristic plot?
I_C against V_CE with I_B held constant.
What happens in the cut-off region?
I_B = 0, I_C = 0, V_CE is maximum, so the transistor is fully OFF.
Maximum I_B and I_C, minimum V_CE, so the transistor is fully ON.
Which region is used for amplification?
The active region (BEJ forward, CBJ reverse).
m2-bjt-gains: Define alpha of a transistor and its range.
α = I_C / I_E. It lies between 0.95 and 0.999 and is always less than 1.
β = I_C / I_B. It can be as high as 500.
Write β in terms of α.
Write α in terms of β.
Express I_E using I_B and β.
Express I_B using I_E and α.
With I_B = 50 µA and β = 100, what are I_C and I_E?
I_C = I_E − I_B, and I_B is never zero, so I_C is slightly smaller than I_E.
m2-mosfet-intro: BJT versus MOSFET: what controls each?
The BJT is current controlled; the MOSFET is voltage controlled (by an electric field).
Why is the MOSFET called unipolar?
Only one kind of carrier conducts: electrons in n-channel, holes in p-channel.
Controls the channel conductivity. It sits on an extremely thin oxide layer.
Why can a MOSFET be treated as a three-terminal device?
The substrate is frequently connected to the source.
What is the difference between enhancement and depletion MOSFETs in terms of the field?
Enhancement: the field increases majority carriers. Depletion: the field reduces them.
What are the source and drain made of in an nMOS?
Heavily doped n regions in a p-type body.
m2-emosfet: Why does an enhancement MOSFET have a broken line in its symbol?
There is no continuous channel between source and drain when the gate voltage is zero.
What is the gate made of and what insulates it?
A thin aluminium layer over a thin SiO2 insulating layer.
Why is the MOSFET input impedance extremely high?
The SiO2 layer insulates the gate from the channel.
Is an enhancement MOSFET normally ON or OFF?
Normally OFF: no drain current at zero gate voltage.
Why is it called an enhancement device?
Increasing the gate voltage increases the drain current, up to the maximum.
What are the three operating regions?
Cut-off (V_GS < V_th), linear/ohmic (V_GS > V_th, acts like a resistor) and saturation/active (V_DS > V_GS − V_th, constant current source).
Which region is used for amplifier circuits?
The metal gate, the SiO2 insulator and the semiconductor channel: a parallel-plate capacitor.
m2-dmosfet: How does a depletion MOSFET differ in construction from an enhancement MOSFET?
A channel is added between the drain and source.
Is a depletion MOSFET normally ON or OFF?
Normally ON: it conducts with no gate voltage.
When is the drain current maximum in a depletion MOSFET?
Why is it called a depletion device?
Increasing the gate voltage depletes the current until it stops.
Why is a depletion MOSFET called dual-mode?
It works with bipolar (positive and negative) gate input signals, giving both depletion and enhancement operation.
Enhancement: no current. Depletion: maximum current.
m2-mosfet-apps: Name two power-electronics uses of MOSFETs.
SMPS (switch-mode power supplies), DC–DC converters, inverters, motor control.
Which technology uses MOSFETs for logic gates in CPUs?
Why are MOSFETs good for hi-fi audio amplifiers?
Name three advantages of a MOSFET.
Higher switching speed, lower power consumption, higher input impedance (also better thermal stability and efficiency at low voltages).
The thin oxide layer can be permanently damaged by electrostatic charge; overload voltages make it unstable.
m2-opamp-intro: A very high gain amplifier with very high input impedance (a few megaohms) and low output impedance (below 100 Ω), built on a difference amplifier with plus and minus inputs.
Why is it called an operational amplifier?
Because it performs operations such as summation, scaling, differentiation and integration.
What happens if the signal goes to the + input (− grounded)?
The output has the same polarity as the input.
What happens if the signal goes to the − input (+ grounded)?
The output is opposite in phase.
What does an op-amp amplify in differential mode?
What is the output in ideal common-mode operation?
0 V: the equal signals cancel. In practice a small output remains.
Which pins are the inputs and output on the 741?
Pin 2 inverting input, pin 3 non-inverting input, pin 6 output. Supplies: pin 7 +Vcc, pin 4 −Vcc.
Why is an op-amp also called a linear integrated circuit?
It performs many linear operations (and some non-linear functions) as an analog IC.
m2-opamp-ideal: Infinite open-loop gain, infinite bandwidth, zero common-mode gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance.
What does infinite input resistance mean for the source?
Almost any signal source can drive it and the source is not loaded.
What does zero output resistance allow?
The output can drive an infinite number of other devices.
Any frequency from 0 to infinity is amplified without attenuation.
The common-mode noise voltage at the output is zero.
What does infinite slew rate mean?
Output changes occur at the same instant as input changes.
m2-opamp-apps: A_v = 1 + R1 / R2 (R1 is the feedback resistor, R2 goes to ground).
What does the minus sign in the inverting gain mean?
The output is 180° out of phase with (inverted from) the input.
A temperature sensor detects fire, the op-amp amplifies its small current, the sprinkler is activated and the water puts out the fire.
With R_i = 10 kΩ and R_f = 100 kΩ what is the gain?
With R1 = 90 kΩ and R2 = 10 kΩ in a non-inverting amplifier, what is the gain?
m2-em-spectrum: The full range of electromagnetic radiation, organised by frequency and wavelength: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.
Do EM waves need a medium?
No. Unlike sound waves, they can travel through empty space.
How fast do EM waves travel in a vacuum?
At the speed of light; all EM waves travel at the same speed.
Name four technologies built on the EM spectrum.
Radios, televisions, mobile phones and microwave ovens.
EM signals above 30 GHz (the EHF band, 30–300 GHz).
What lies above the millimetre-wave region?
The optical spectrum: infrared, visible and ultraviolet light.
m2-freq-bands: Range of ELF and a common use?
30 to 300 Hz. AC power line frequencies (50 and 60 Hz).
Range of the voice frequency band?
300 to 3000 Hz, the normal range of human speech.
What is the VLF band used for in the navy?
Communicating with submarines. VLF is 3 to 30 kHz.
Which band is used for AM radio and what are its limits?
MF (300 to 3000 kHz). AM broadcasting is 535 to 1605 kHz.
Which band is called short waves?
HF, 3 to 30 MHz.
Which band carries FM broadcasting?
VHF (30 to 300 MHz); FM is 88 to 108 MHz.
Which band carries cellular telephones and UHF TV?
UHF, 300 to 3000 MHz.
What frequency does a microwave oven usually use?
What are SHF and EHF ranges?
SHF 3 to 30 GHz (satellite, radar, wireless LAN); EHF 30 to 300 GHz (millimetre waves).
What are subcarriers?
Signals modulated by the baseband information, used in the LF range. Two or more are added and the combination modulates the final high-frequency carrier.
m2-optical: What are the three types of light wave?
0.4 to 0.8 µm (400 to 800 nm), about 4000 Å (violet) to 8000 Å (red).
1 Å = 10^-10 m, used for light wavelengths.
Which has the shorter wavelength, red or violet light?
Violet (high frequency); red is low frequency and long wavelength.
No. Its main use is medical. Solar UV causes sunburn.
About 0.1 mm to 700 nm (100 to 0.7 µm).
m2-comm-system: What three elements does every electronic communication system have?
A transmitter, a communication channel (medium) and a receiver.
Any phenomenon that degrades or interferes with the transmitted information. It is added in the channel and in the receiver.
What does an input transducer do?
Converts a physical quantity such as sound, temperature or pressure into a time-varying electrical signal (a microphone in radio).
What is the main function of a transmitter?
Modulation: superimposing the message signal on a high-frequency carrier, for a signal suitable for the medium.
What circuits are inside a transmitter?
Oscillators, amplifiers, tuned circuits and filters, modulators, frequency mixers and frequency synthesizers.
Reproduces the message signal in electrical form from the distorted received signal. A demodulator recovers the intelligence from the carrier.
What is a transceiver? Give examples.
Transmitter and receiver in a single housing sharing circuits such as the power supply: telephones, handheld radios, cellular phones, modems.
What does an output transducer do?
Delivers the original signal in readable form, e.g. a speaker for voice or an LCD for video.
m2-comm-channels: The medium by which the electronic signal is sent from one place to another.
Wire conductors, fibre-optic cable and free space.
Free space is the medium (wireless). It uses the EM spectrum.
How does optical fibre carry digital data?
Information is converted to digital form that turns a laser diode on and off at high speed.
Difference between passive and active sonar?
Passive sonar listens with hydrophones. Active sonar sends out and uses the echo, like radar, to find range and direction.
Signals added to the AC line voltage (carrier current transmission), used for remote control and some LANs.
Give examples of electrical conductor channels.
A pair of wires, coaxial cable (cable TV) and twisted-pair cable (LAN).
m2-modulation: Superimposing a low-frequency information signal on a high-frequency carrier for efficient long-distance transmission. Done at the transmitter.
Why can the message not be sent directly over long distances?
Its frequency and amplitude are too low.
Reduce antenna height, allow multiplexing, enable long-distance communication, reduce noise and signal interference.
Extracting the original information from the modulated carrier at the receiving end, using a demodulator.
What varies in AM, FM and PM?
AM: amplitude of the carrier. FM: frequency. PM: phase angle.
Which modulation is preferred for long distance?
AM. FM and PM are preferred for short distance.
The result of superimposing the message on the carrier; the wave that is transmitted.
m2-cell-basics: What is the basic idea of a cellular system?
Divide the service area into many small cells, each with its own low-power transmitter and receiver, instead of one big transmitter.
Mobile telephone switching office: controls all cells and links them to the main telephone system.
The automatic switching of a call from a weaker cell to a stronger one as the user moves, decided by the MTSO computer.
Advanced Mobile Phone System, the original US analog FM cell system, replaced by 2G, 3G and 4G digital systems.
What decides the number of cells in an area?
The density of users: many small cells in cities, fewer in rural areas.
A group of adjacent cells, usually 7, with no frequency reuse inside it.
Macrocell ~6 miles wide (remote, high power); microcell ~half a mile (urban, low power); picocell covers a building or tunnel.
When was the first commercial cellular service launched?
1979, by the Nordic Mobile Telephone in Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark.
m2-cell-freq: What are the original cellular uplink and downlink bands?
Uplink 824 to 849 MHz (reverse channels); downlink 869 to 894 MHz (forward channels).
How wide is each cellular block and how many channels did it have originally?
25 MHz, divided into 832 channels of 30 kHz.
Two 60 MHz blocks: 1850–1910 MHz (uplink) and 1930–1990 MHz (downlink).
Why use higher microwave frequencies for cell phones?
More system capacity (more subscribers) and smaller antennas, though the range is somewhat less.
Which bands are most used in Europe?
What is the direction of uplink and downlink?
Uplink: phone to base station. Downlink: base station to phone.
m2-cell-network: 1G analog voice (AMPS); 2G digital voice, more efficient (GSM, US-TDMA); 3G high-speed voice integrated with data (GPRS, CDMA).
5G: faster speeds, lower latency, massive device connectivity. 6G: up to 1 Tbps (about 50× 5G), ultra-low latency, AI integration.
Base Transceiver Station, the main component of a cell, connecting subscribers to the network through antennas.
Interface between BTSs; routes calls between BTSs and to the MSC.
Mobile Switching Center: coordinator of the network, routes calls between BSCs and links to other networks (PSTN).
HLR: permanent subscriber data kept by the provider. VLR: temporary data kept in the MSC where the subscriber currently is.
What is stored in the EIR and AuC?
EIR: identifies phones by IMEI. AuC: authorised subscriber list, checks identity and gives encryption parameters.
m2-sat-basics: What does a communication satellite do?
Acts as a relay station (RF repeater) for earth sources, retransmitting signals through a transponder.
Why put the antenna on a satellite?
To overcome the line-of-sight limit (about 45–55 km) of ground communication.
How high is a geostationary satellite and why does it look fixed?
About 35,900 km up; its rotation is synchronised with the Earth.
What are the three stages of satellite communication?
What is the ground and space segment?
Ground segment: earth stations and terrestrial systems. Space segment: the satellite.
Name two advantages and two disadvantages.
Advantages: every corner of the Earth covered, the user controls the network. Disadvantages: high initial cost, blockage of frequencies, interference.
Name a few uses of satellite communication.
Telephone, television, digital cinema, radio, amateur radio, internet, military, disaster management.
m2-sat-transponder: What are the basic functions of a transponder?
Why must a transponder translate frequency?
It cannot transmit and receive on the same frequency: its strong transmit signal would desensitize the receiver and block the weak uplink signal.
Typical uplink and downlink frequencies in the C band?
About 6 GHz up (5.925–6.425) and 4 GHz down (3.7–4.2).
14–14.5 GHz up and 11.7–12.2 GHz down (14/12 GHz).
Why are newer satellites moving to Ku band?
The C band is overcrowded and has interference; Ku gives higher antenna gain for the same size.
What are X and L bands used for?
X: military satellites and radar. L: navigation, marine and aeronautical communication, radar.
What is the satellite’s communication subsystem?
A set of transponders supported by housekeeping subsystems: power, telemetry/tracking/command, antennas, propulsion, attitude stabilization.
Example of channel count on a satellite?
m2-radar: What does RADAR stand for?
RAdio Detection And Ranging.
How is the range of a target measured?
From the time the signal takes to reach the object and return as an echo.
How does radar find the speed of a moving target?
By the Doppler shift in the frequency of the echo, proportional to the radial velocity.
How is the location of a stationary object found?
From the angle the antenna points at when the echo has maximum amplitude.
What does the duplexer do?
Isolates the transmitter and receiver so a single antenna serves both.
What does the pulse modulator do?
Switches the power amplifier on and off according to the pulses from the waveform generator.
What is the role of the IF amplifier?
Amplifies the IF pulse, acts as a matched filter, increases SNR and sets the receiver bandwidth.
What does the threshold decision stage do?
Decides if a target exists by comparing the signal level with a set threshold.
What is a PPI?
Plan Position Indicator, a CRT display that maps range and location in polar coordinates.
Name four radar applications.
Military, air traffic control, ship safety, remote sensing (weather, agriculture, pollution).
m4-mfg-intro: Conversion of raw material into a useful product.
What mainly decides the choice of manufacturing process?
The material and the shape of the part.
Name the five families of manufacturing methods.
Metal casting, metal forming, machining, joining processes, powder metallurgy.
Which family removes material from a larger block?
Which family deforms solid metal into shape?
Metal forming: extrusion, forging and rolling.
m4-sand-casting: Why is sand casting called an expendable mould process?
The mould is temporary and non-reusable: it is broken to take out the solidified cast.
What is moulding sand made of?
A mixture of silica sand, clay and moisture, which must keep its permeability.
What is the drag, the cope and the cheek?
Drag = lower flask, cope = upper flask, cheek = intermediate flask.
What is the job of a riser?
A column of molten metal that feeds the casting as it shrinks.
Sprue: passage by which metal reaches the cavity. Runner: channel carrying metal from the sprue to the gate.
A generally baked part of the mould used to create cavities.
Give the five steps of sand casting.
Place pattern, add gating system, remove pattern and pour, cool and solidify, break mould and remove cast.
Where should the parting line be chosen?
Along a flat plane rather than a contoured one, for economical casting.
m4-casting-design: Where should a riser be attached?
To the heaviest section; surrounding sections should be thinner.
The thinnest, farthest from the riser. Solidification then moves toward the heaviest section and the riser.
What four things must pattern construction allow for?
Mould parting line, machined surfaces, shrinkage of the material and draft.
A taper on the pattern that helps it come out of the mould.
Metal spacers that support a core: they prevent core sag before pouring and core float after pouring.
Which pattern makes several identical castings in one mould?
What is a match plate pattern?
The cope and drag halves of the pattern are mounted on opposite sides of a plate.
When is a skeleton pattern used?
To create moulds for simple, large castings.
m4-casting-defects: Improper alignment of the mould cavities on the cope and drag.
Improper mould strength and a high pouring temperature.
Low pouring temperature and lack of fluidity.
What causes hot tears or hot cracks?
Intersecting sections solidify together and retard solidification, giving porosity and shrinkage cavities.
m4-extrusion: Long parts of uniform cross section, such as cylindrical bars and hollow tubes.
Heat the billet, insert it into a container, force it through a die hole, get the desired cross section.
Why is most extrusion done hot?
The flow stress of the metal is lower at high temperature.
Which metals extrude more easily: aluminium or steel?
Aluminium. Extrudability is in reverse order of strength: Al, Cu, Mg, Zn alloys are above steels.
What is cold extrusion good for?
No oxidation, higher strength from cold working, closer tolerances and better surface finish.
The billet is surrounded by a pressurised liquid: less friction, more ductility at high pressure, even flow, no residue on walls.
Circumscribing-circle diameter, the measure of extrusion capacity.
What limits the largest extrudable section?
Press tonnage, the material and the complexity of the cross section.
m4-forging: What does forging do to voids and pores?
Eliminates cavities, voids and pores, and gives more strength and structural integrity.
Thin sections, large changes in cross-sectional area, and shapes needing a cranked parting line.
What is a web in forging?
The wall filled by horizontal flow, perpendicular to die motion and parallel to the parting plane.
What is a rib or boss?
Any wall filled by flow parallel to the die motion.
A small web area surrounded by thicker metal.
Why is parting line location critical?
It determines die cost, draft requirements, grain flow and trimming procedures.
The directional pattern metal crystals take during plastic deformation.
Why is draft greater on inside surfaces?
The part shrinks onto die projections as it cools.
m4-rolling: Metal is plastically deformed between rotating rolls, reducing thickness and changing cross section.
Volume: thinner means longer and wider.
Large rolls supporting smaller work rolls in high-load applications.
I-sections, H-sections, angle (L) sections, channel (U) sections.
Better finish and closer tolerances, true and square bars, better tube concentricity and straightness.
m4-hot-cold: Hot vs cold working: how is the line drawn?
Hot is above the recrystallisation temperature, cold is below it.
Which needs more force: hot or cold working?
Cold working. Hot working forms none.
Hot working; cold working wears tools more.
Why does hot working use more energy?
The metal has to be heated.
m4-welding-basics: A materials joining process that produces coalescence by heating to suitable temperatures, with or without pressure, or by pressure alone, and with or without filler material.
Merging of materials to form a single, unified piece.
Name the three regions of a welded butt joint.
Base metal (BM), fusion zone (FZ) and heat affected zone (HAZ).
What decides the properties of the fusion zone?
Mainly the filler metal deposited there.
Which region is the weakest and why?
The HAZ: its microstructure is altered and it softens, so it is weaker than both BM and FZ.
Does the blue oxidation colour on a pipe weld show the HAZ width?
No. It is oxidation at about 316 °C; the HAZ is the narrow area immediately around the weld.
m4-welding-classes: Name the four groups of commercial welding processes.
Gas welding, electric arc welding, power beam (high density) welding, solid state welding.
Which processes are power beam welding?
Electron beam welding (EBW) and laser beam welding (LBW).
Which processes are solid state welding?
Friction stir welding (FSW), friction welding (FW) and resistance welding (RSW).
SMAW, GTAW, GMAW, PAW, FCAW, SAW, ESW.
Power density and temperature of gas, arc and beam welding?
Gas about 10 W/cm² and 3300 °C; arc about 50 W/cm² and 6000 °C; beam about 10000 W/cm² and 20000 to 30000 °C.
What do higher energy densities give?
Lower heat losses and greater arc efficiency; also more penetration, speed and quality, at higher equipment cost.
m4-arc-welding: Straight polarity: about two-thirds of the power is at the work end, giving a narrow, deep weld.
Reverse polarity: heating at the tungsten electrode, shallow weld, used on thin sheets of oxide-forming materials.
Why does DCEP clean the weld surface?
Positive ions of the shielding gas bombard the workpiece and knock off oxide films.
Good penetration and oxide cleaning action both.
More penetration in the fusion zone.
What happens if arc length changes too much?
Less depth of penetration, but higher productivity, less heat input, less distortion and residual stress.
Larger needs more current and gives a high deposition rate; smaller gives lower deposition rate and higher current density.
m4-weld-joints: Butt, lap, T, edge and corner joints.
Sheet metal fabrication, particularly under 3 mm thickness: tanks, boxes, metal enclosures.
What does a corner joint form?
An L-shape, joining two pieces at a right angle; used in box construction and frames.
Thickness below 5 mm; no bevelling needed.
Single V or U butt joint: thickness?
Double V or U butt joint: thickness?
What are the welding positions called?
It causes distortion and raises time and cost, and does not improve strength.
m4-gtaw-gmaw: What is GTAW and its old name?
Gas tungsten arc welding, formerly TIG (tungsten inert gas).
No. It is a tungsten electrode with 1–2% thorium oxide.
What metals is TIG mostly used on?
Aluminium alloys, magnesium alloys and stainless steel.
Melting at the peak current; at the low level the arc stays but little heat goes in, so the weld cools.
Yes. MIG (GMAW) has a higher deposition rate than TIG.
Which process is used for root passes and which for fill passes?
Root passes with TIG, fill passes with MIG.
Shielding gas for TIG and MIG?
TIG: pure argon. MIG: typically 75% argon and 25% CO2.
Lower deposition rate and the need for more experienced welders.
m4-machining-basics: Subtractive manufacturing: removing material from a larger block to get the desired shape and finish.
What does a horizontal bar on a surface symbol mean?
Material removal by machining is required.
Single point has one cutting edge (turning, boring, shaping, planing); multi-point has two or more (milling cutters, drill, reamer, broach, grinding wheel).
What must a cutting tool be made of?
A material harder than the work, with more material behind the cutting edge.
Where does most cutting heat go?
Mostly into the chips (shear zone); about 10–20% into the tool and 3–5% into the workpiece.
Continuous, continuous with built-up edge, discontinuous, serrated or segmented.
m4-hole-making: Slab milling, tapping, drilling, grinding, boring.
What follows drilling for better finish and accuracy?
Enlarging an existing hole, typically after drilling, for accurate or tapered internal diameters.
A chip-producing threading tool with multiple cutting teeth; it cuts internal threads.
m4-turning-milling: A single point tool removes material from a rotating workpiece to make cylinders, usually on a lathe.
Distance the tool travels per revolution of the workpiece (mm/rev).
The perpendicular distance the tool penetrates the workpiece in a single pass (mm).
Slab: cutter axis parallel to the workpiece. Face: cutter axis perpendicular.
What is end milling used for?
Milling slots; the cutter has edges on its periphery and tip.
Down milling gives a better finish and longer tool life.
Shaping: tool reciprocates, small jobs. Planing: workpiece reciprocates, large jobs.
Workpiece supported by a blade and a regulating wheel instead of centres.
m4-cnc: Computer numerical control: controlling machine movements by coded numerical instructions, introduced in the early 1950s.
Name four things CNC can control.
Spindle on/off, tool changing, tool or workpiece paths, cutting fluid on/off.
Point-to-point control: what happens and where is it used?
Tool moves at maximum velocity then decelerates near the target; used in drilling, punching and straight milling.
Contouring control: where is it used?
Milling, turning, engraving and profile cutting; positioning and operation along controlled paths.
Data input, data processing, data output (pulsed commands to the servomotor).
Hub turned and faced, mounting and convection holes drilled, pad contact area faced.
m4-am-intro: What does AM stand for and what does it do?
Additive manufacturing: builds parts layer by layer, ideal for complex, light weight shapes.
What are the advantages of AM named in the course?
Complex geometries, part consolidation, less scrap, light weighting.
How does STL describe a surface?
With triangles, each given by three points and a facet normal vector pointing outward.
Name the three phases of the AM sequence.
Digital phase, manufacturing phase, post processing phase.
Removal from the machine, support removal, GD&T analysis, testing and evaluation.
m4-am-categories: Who classifies AM into seven categories?
ASTM (American Society for Testing and Materials).
Material extrusion, vat photopolymerisation, powder bed fusion, binder jetting, material jetting, directed energy deposition, sheet lamination.
Powder bed fusion: material, energy, examples?
Powder, laser or e-beam, SLS and SLM.
What is DED mainly used for?
Repairing high-value parts, such as aerospace turbine blades, and adding features.
What must binder-jetted parts get afterwards?
Sintering, infiltration or curing to strengthen them.
Adhesive, ultrasonic welding or thermal bonding; sheets are cut to shape (LOM, UAM).
How should the AM process be selected?
Match the product needs: material, accuracy, strength, volume and cost.
m4-fdm: Fused deposition modelling / fused filament fabrication: heated filament is extruded layer by layer. Developed by Stratasys, USA.
Thermoplastic filaments such as ABS and PLA.
Design (CAD, STL, slicing to G-code), printing, post processing.
